assembly: Carpenter fits on site with a printed guide; about 45 minutes per wardrobe (assumption).

bom.item: adjustable floor foot with shield lip

construction_sequence: Set unit with a 30 mm wall gap
Fix wall brackets with anchors suited to the wall
failure_modes: Anchors pull out of weak walls
Carpenter bridges the gap with trims or filler
Termites climb hidden inside feet if the shield lip is missing
functional_principles: Break hidden contact between wall or floor and the furniture carcass
Make any termite mud tube cross visible metal so it can be seen early
Carry the unit's load and prevent tipping
low_cost_validation: Have a local fabricator make 2 sets for about ₹3,000 (assumption), load test with sandbags, and install in 2 volunteer homes with a termite history.
maintenance: Remove the plinth every 6 months and look for mud tubes on metal.

material_options.cons: Zinc coating damaged at cut edges
material_options.pros: Cheap, strong, local fabricators can make it

production_comparison.notes: hacksaw, drill and vice for the first prototypes
laser or punch press at a job shop
local fabricators can bend and drill
levelling feet and anchors bought in

prototype_dimensions: Wall bracket: 2 mm GI, 60 x 60 mm legs, 40 mm wide, 30 mm standoff. Floor foot: 40 mm diameter, 30 mm high, M10 leveller, 60 mm shield lip.
safety_requirements: Anchor type matched to brick, block or AAC wall
Structural review for tall or overhead units
technical_requirements: Hold a loaded 2.1 m wardrobe (estimate 150 kg, to be checked) with a safety factor of at least 3
Anti-tip restraint on every tall unit
Gap 25-40 mm, kept clear of trims and fillers
Galvanised or stainless parts for humid interiors
Floor feet with a metal shield lip so termites cannot climb hidden
tests: Static load at 3x expected load for 24 hours
Anchor pull-out tests in brick and AAC
Observation in 2 homes with past termite activity for 6 months
tolerances: Hole positions +/-0.5 mm; bend angle +/-1 degree; standoff gap 30 +/-3 mm.
